{{Short description|Canadian mathematician}}
'''Clement Wing Hong Lam''' ({{zh|c=林永康}}) is a Canadian mathematician, specializing in [[combinatorics]]. He is famous for the computer proof, with Larry Thiel and S. Swiercz, of the nonexistence of a [[finite projective plane]] of order 10.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Clement W. H. Lam |author2=Larry Thiel |author3=S. Swiercz |title=The Nonexistence of Finite Projective Planes of Order 10|journal=Can. J. Math.|volume=41|issue=6 |year=1989|pages=1117–1123|doi=10.4153/cjm-1989-049-4}}</ref>

Lam earned his PhD in 1974 under [[Herbert Ryser]] at [[Caltech]] with thesis ''Rational G-Circulants Satisfying the Matrix Equation <math>A^2=d I+\lambda J</math>''.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=11894}}</ref> He is a professor at [[Concordia University]] in [[Montreal]].

In 2006 he received the [[Euler medal]]. In 1992 he received the [[Lester Randolph Ford Award]] for the article ''The search for a finite projective plane of order 10''.<ref>{{cite journal|title=The search for a finite projective plane of order 10|journal=Amer. Math. Monthly|volume=98|issue=4|year=1991|pages=305–318|doi=10.2307/2323798 | url = https://www.maa.org/programs/maa-awards/writing-awards/the-search-for-a-finite-projective-plane-of-order-10|jstor=2323798|last1=Lam|first1=C. W. H.|url-access=subscription}}</ref> The eponymous [[Lam's problem]] is equivalent to finding a finite projective plane of order 10 or finding 9 orthogonal [[Latin square]]s of order 10.<ref>[http://mathworld.wolfram.com/LamsProblem.html Lam´s Problem at Mathworld]</ref>
